claim: Brown adipose tissue (BAT) is composed of thermogenic cells that convert chemical energy into heat to maintain a constant body temperature and counteract metabolic disease.
source: Brown adipose tissue (BAT) is composed of thermogenic cells that convert chemical energy into heat to maintain a constant body temperature and counteract metabolic disease.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about BAT function.

claim: Cold exposure revealed changes in pathways involved in amino acid, glucose, and TCA cycle metabolism in brown adipose tissue.
source: Transcriptome and metabolome analysis revealed changes in pathways involved in amino acid, glucose, and TCA cycle metabolism.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental transcriptome and metabolome analysis data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Activated brown adipocytes increased labeling of pyruvate and TCA cycle intermediates from U13C-glucose.
source: Using isotopic labeling experiments, we found that activated brown adipocytes increased labeling of pyruvate and TCA cycle intermediates from U13C-glucose.
evidence: This is supported by isotopic labeling experimental data shown in the manuscript.

claim: Mitochondrial pyruvate uptake is essential for optimal thermogenesis.
source: We show that mitochondrial pyruvate uptake is essential for optimal thermogenesis, as conditional deletion of Mpc1 in brown adipocytes leads to impaired cold adaptation.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from conditional deletion of Mpc1 in brown adipocytes.

claim: Conditional deletion of Mpc1 in brown adipocytes leads to impaired cold adaptation.
source: We show that mitochondrial pyruvate uptake is essential for optimal thermogenesis, as conditional deletion of Mpc1 in brown adipocytes leads to impaired cold adaptation.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing cold sensitivity in Mpc1 knockout mice.

claim: Loss of MPC1 led to impaired labeling of TCA cycle intermediates from U13C-glucose.
source: Isotopic labeling experiments using U13C-glucose showed that loss of MPC1 led to impaired labeling of TCA cycle intermediates.
evidence: This is supported by isotopic labeling experimental data in MPC1 knockout cells.

claim: Loss of MPC1 in BAT increased 3-hydroxybutyrate levels in blood and BAT in response to the cold.
source: Loss of MPC1 in BAT increased 3-hydroxybutyrate levels in blood and BAT in response to the cold, suggesting that ketogenesis provides an alternative fuel source to compensate.
evidence: This is supported by metabolomics data showing elevated 3-hydroxybutyrate levels.

claim: Ketogenesis provides an alternative fuel source to compensate for loss of MPC1.
source: Loss of MPC1 in BAT increased 3-hydroxybutyrate levels in blood and BAT in response to the cold, suggesting that ketogenesis provides an alternative fuel source to compensate.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed increase in 3-hydroxybutyrate levels.

claim: Complete glucose oxidation is essential for optimal brown fat thermogenesis.
source: Collectively, these studies highlight that complete glucose oxidation is essential for optimal brown fat thermogenesis.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data showing impaired thermogenesis when glucose oxidation is blocked.

claim: Brown adipose tissue (BAT) thermogenesis is an energy demanding process that has been key to the evolution and survival of mammals.
source: Brown adipose tissue (BAT) thermogenesis is an energy demanding process that has been key to the evolution and survival of mammals (Gaudry et al., 2019; Oelkrug et al., 2015; Barnett and Dickson, 1989).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Mechanisms that promote energy expenditure in the cold will provide attractive therapeutic interventions to treating metabolic diseases associated with obesity.
source: With the excess calorie intake associated with a western diet, mechanisms that promote energy expenditure in the cold will provide attractive therapeutic interventions to treating metabolic diseases associated with obesity (Cypess et al., 2009; Vijgen et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature and represents a speculative therapeutic application.

claim: Cold exposure triggers the activation of the sympathetic nervous system to secrete norepinephrine, which signals through the β3-adrenergic receptor (β3-AR) and stimulates production of cyclic AMP (cAMP).
source: Cold exposure triggers the activation of the sympathetic nervous system to secrete norepinephrine, which signals through the β3-adrenergic receptor (β3-AR) and stimulates production of cyclic AMP (cAMP) (Townsend and Tseng, 2014; Londos et al., 1985).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: cAMP promotes the activation of protein kinase A (PKA), which in turn upregulates transcription of thermogenic pathways and leads to the activation of lipolysis.
source: cAMP promotes the activation of protein kinase A (PKA), which in turn upregulates transcription of thermogenic pathways and leads to the activation of lipolysis (Cannon and Nedergaard, 2004; Zhang et al., 2005).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Free fatty acids released can directly activate Uncoupling Protein 1 (UCP1), which uncouples the electron transport chain to generate heat.
source: Free fatty acids released can directly activate Uncoupling Protein 1 (UCP1), which uncouples the electron transport chain to generate heat (Fedorenko et al., 2012; Klaus et al., 1991; Busiello et al., 2015).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Cold exposure stimulates uptake of both glucose, triglyceride(TG)-rich lipoproteins and free fatty acids from the blood.
source: Cold exposure stimulates uptake of both glucose, triglyceride(TG)-rich lipoproteins and free fatty acids from the blood (Labbé et al., 2015; Heine et al., 2018; Ferré et al., 1986).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Human brown fat was only believed to be found in newborns, but now we appreciate that adults have brown adipose tissue, a discovery that was made through use of glucose tracer (18F-fluorodeoxyglucose) and positron-emission tomographic and computed tomographic (PET–CT) scans.
source: Human brown fat was only believed to be found in newborns, but now we appreciate that adults have brown adipose tissue, a discovery that was made through use of glucose tracer (18F-fluorodeoxyglucose) and positron-emission tomographic and computed tomographic (PET–CT) scans (Cypess et al., 2009; Virtanen et al., 2009).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Cold exposure could lower blood glucose levels in adults.
source: In addition, it was previously recognized that cold exposure could lower blood glucose levels in adults (Martineau and Jacobs, 1989).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: siRNAs targeting Slc2a1 (GLUT1), Slc2a4 (GLUT4), Hk2 (hexokinase2), or Pkm (pyruvate kinase, muscle) demonstrated the importance of glycolysis, as β3-AR agonist failed to increase glucose uptake and oxygen consumption in these cells.
source: The role of glucose uptake on metabolism has been explored in vitro using immortalized brown adipocytes where siRNAs targeting Slc2a1 (GLUT1), Slc2a4 (GLUT4), Hk2 (hexokinase2), or Pkm (pyruvate kinase, muscle) (enzymes catalyzing the first and the last step of glycolysis) demonstrated the importance of glycolysis, as β3-AR agonist failed to increase glucose uptake and oxygen consumption in these cells (Winther et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: There is no adequate in vivo model demonstrating the importance of BAT glycolysis or glucose oxidation on adaptive thermogenesis.
source: However, there is no adequate in vivo model demonstrating the importance of BAT glycolysis or glucose oxidation on adaptive thermogenesis.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of the field based on knowledge of existing literature.

claim: MPC is a multimeric complex in the inner mitochondrial membrane that consists of MPC1 and MPC2 subunits.
source: MPC is a multimeric complex in the inner mitochondrial membrane that consists of MPC1 and MPC2 subunits (Bricker et al., 2012; Herzig et al., 2012; Schell et al., 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Deletion of either MPC1 or MPC2 subunit leads to instability of a functional MPC complex.
source: Deletion of either subunit leads to instability of a functional MPC complex.
evidence: This is established knowledge about MPC complex stability.

claim: MPC links the end product of glycolysis to glucose oxidation by transporting pyruvate into the mitochondrial matrix.
source: MPC links the end product of glycolysis to glucose oxidation by transporting pyruvate into the mitochondrial matrix (Mowbray, 1975).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: Loss-of-function studies targeting MPC1 or MPC2 has been shown to limit mitochondrial pyruvate transport in yeast, flies and mammals.
source: Loss-of-function studies targeting MPC1 or MPC2 has been shown to limit mitochondrial pyruvate transport in yeast, flies and mammals (Herzig et al., 2012; Bricker et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Once in the mitochondria, pyruvate is decarboxylated to acetyl-CoA for further processing in the TCA cycle to generate NADH and fuel ATP production by OXPHOS complexes.
source: Once in the mitochondria, pyruvate is decarboxylated to acetyl-CoA for further processing in the TCA cycle to generate NADH and fuel ATP production by OXPHOS complexes.
evidence: This is established knowledge about pyruvate metabolism.

claim: Cytosolic pyruvate can be reduced to lactate by lactate dehydrogenase complex A (LDHA), a process commonly upregulated in cancer cells.
source: Alternatively, cytosolic pyruvate can be reduced to lactate by lactate dehydrogenase complex A (LDHA), a process commonly upregulated in cancer cells (Vander Heiden et al., 2009).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: Cold exposure or direct stimulation of β3-AR stimulates glucose utilization by BAT in both humans and rodents.
source: While it is clear that cold exposure or direct stimulation of β3-AR stimulates glucose utilization by BAT in both humans (Cypess et al., 2009; Saito et al., 2009) and rodents (Mirbolooki et al., 2014; Vallerand et al., 1990), it is not clear how important glucose oxidation is during thermogenesis nor what the metabolic fate of glucose is in activated BAT.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Activation of BAT led to increased levels of the TCA cycle intermediate succinate.
source: Recently, comparative metabolomics analysis has shown that activation of BAT led to increased levels of the TCA cycle intermediate succinate; however, it is unclear whether glucose-derived TCA cycle intermediates are required for thermogenesis (Mills et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: 1907 transcripts were upregulated with cold exposure in BAT.
source: We found that 1907 transcripts were upregulated with cold exposure, while 3273 were decreased (Supplementary file 1 and supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is supported by RNA sequencing data.

claim: 3273 transcripts were decreased with cold exposure in BAT.
source: We found that 1907 transcripts were upregulated with cold exposure, while 3273 were decreased (Supplementary file 1 and supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is supported by RNA sequencing data.

claim: Cold exposure stimulated distinct transcriptional changes in BAT that involve various aspects of metabolism including induction of glucose metabolic process, sphingolipid metabolism, amino acid metabolism, and cellular respiration.
source: Using Gene Set Enrichment Analysis (GSEA), we found that cold exposure stimulated distinct transcriptional changes in BAT that involve various aspects of metabolism. Notable changes include induction of glucose metabolic process, sphingolipid metabolism, amino acid metabolism, and cellular respiration, while pathways involved in cell cycle control, DNA repair, and glycoprotein metabolism were downregulated (Figure 1A and B).
evidence: This is supported by GSEA analysis of RNA sequencing data shown in Figure 1A and B.

claim: Pathways involved in cell cycle control, DNA repair, and glycoprotein metabolism were downregulated with cold exposure in BAT.
source: Using Gene Set Enrichment Analysis (GSEA), we found that cold exposure stimulated distinct transcriptional changes in BAT that involve various aspects of metabolism. Notable changes include induction of glucose metabolic process, sphingolipid metabolism, amino acid metabolism, and cellular respiration, while pathways involved in cell cycle control, DNA repair, and glycoprotein metabolism were downregulated (Figure 1A and B).
evidence: This is supported by GSEA analysis of RNA sequencing data shown in Figure 1A and B.

claim: The BAT metabolome showed elevated levels of glycolytic intermediates, TCA cycle intermediates, ketone bodies, and branched chain amino acids when mice were challenged with the cold.
source: The BAT metabolome showed elevated levels of glycolytic intermediates, TCA cycle intermediates, ketone bodies, and branched chain amino acids when mice were challenged with the cold (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by GC-MS metabolomics data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Amino acids like tyrosine, alanine, threonine, and tryptophan were increased in BAT with cold exposure.
source: Notably, amino acids like tyrosine, alanine, threonine, and tryptophan were increased in BAT, while their levels decreased in serum with cold exposure.
evidence: This is supported by metabolomics data.

claim: Tyrosine, alanine, threonine, and tryptophan levels decreased in serum with cold exposure.
source: Notably, amino acids like tyrosine, alanine, threonine, and tryptophan were increased in BAT, while their levels decreased in serum with cold exposure.
evidence: This is supported by metabolomics data.

claim: BAT uptake could lead to depletion of tyrosine, alanine, threonine, and tryptophan in the blood.
source: Perhaps, BAT uptake could lead to their depletion in the blood.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the observed changes in amino acid levels.

claim: Branched chain amino acids, including Valine, Leucine, and Isoleucine were elevated in BAT with cold exposure.
source: Similar to a recent report (Yoneshiro et al., 2019), we observed that branched chain amino acids, including Valine, Leucine, and Isoleucine were elevated in BAT, while only Leucine and Valine were upregulated in serum (Figure 1C and E).
evidence: This is supported by metabolomics data shown in Figure 1C and E, and is consistent with a cited report.

claim: Only Leucine and Valine were upregulated in serum with cold exposure.
source: Similar to a recent report (Yoneshiro et al., 2019), we observed that branched chain amino acids, including Valine, Leucine, and Isoleucine were elevated in BAT, while only Leucine and Valine were upregulated in serum (Figure 1C and E).
evidence: This is supported by metabolomics data shown in Figure 1C and E.

claim: Both BAT and serum were enriched for pathways involved in amino acid, fatty acid, nucleotide, and glucose metabolism with cold exposure.
source: Both BAT and serum were enriched for pathways involved in amino acid, fatty acid, nucleotide, and glucose metabolism.
evidence: This is supported by MSEA analysis of metabolomics data.

claim: Glucose and pyruvate levels in BAT were elevated in response to 4°C.
source: Notably, glucose and pyruvate levels in BAT were elevated in response to 4°C, while both glucose and pyruvate levels were similar between mice housed at 30°C and 23°C.
evidence: This is supported by metabolomics data.

claim: Glucose and pyruvate levels in BAT were similar between mice housed at 30°C and 23°C.
source: Notably, glucose and pyruvate levels in BAT were elevated in response to 4°C, while both glucose and pyruvate levels were similar between mice housed at 30°C and 23°C.
evidence: This is supported by metabolomics data.

claim: There is an increase in the rate of pyruvate synthesis in response to the cold.
source: This finding would suggest that there is an increase in the rate of pyruvate synthesis in response to the cold (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed increase in pyruvate levels.

claim: Activation of brown adipocytes treated with CL-316,243 had significant 13C-glucose-derived M+3 isotopologues of 13C-Pyruvate, 13C-Lactate and 13C-Glycerol-3-Phosphate.
source: In vitro tracing experiments using [U-13C]-Glucose showed that activation of brown adipocytes treated with CL-316,243 had significant 13C-glucose-derived M+3 isotopologues of 13C-Pyruvate, 13C-Lactate and 13C-Glycerol-3-Phosphate.
evidence: This is supported by isotopic tracing experimental data.

claim: Differentiated brown adipocytes that were treated with CL-316,243 had more than 50% of pyruvate and lactate labeled from [U-13C]-glucose.
source: Differentiated brown adipocytes that were treated with CL-316,243 had more than 50% of pyruvate and lactate labeled.
evidence: This is supported by isotopic tracing experimental data.

claim: There was little alanine labeling from [U-13C]-glucose, despite the rise in M+3 13C-Alanine in response to β3-AR activation.
source: Surprisingly, there was little alanine labeling from [U-13C]-glucose, despite the rise in M+3 13C-Alanine in response to β3-AR activation (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by isotopic tracing experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: There was depletion of M+6 glucose in the media after CL-316,243 administration.
source: During incubation with [U-13C]-Glucose, there was depletion of M+6 glucose in the media after CL-316,243 administration, while M+3 pyruvate in the media increased, but did not respond to CL-316,243 treatment (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by isotopic tracing experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: M+3 pyruvate in the media increased, but did not respond to CL-316,243 treatment.
source: During incubation with [U-13C]-Glucose, there was depletion of M+6 glucose in the media after CL-316,243 administration, while M+3 pyruvate in the media increased, but did not respond to CL-316,243 treatment (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by isotopic tracing experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: CL-316,243 increased the release of M+3 lactate into the media when compared to vehicle.
source: To test whether M+3 lactate derived from [U-13C]-Glucose was being released into the media, we measured media M+3 lactate, and found that CL-316,243 increased the release of M+3 lactate into the media when compared to vehicle (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by isotopic tracing experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Activation of thermogenesis in brown adipocytes leads to increased lactate synthesis and secretion.
source: These results suggest that activation of thermogenesis in brown adipocytes leads to increased lactate synthesis and secretion.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed increase in lactate labeling and release.

claim: Both Mpc1 and Mpc2 expression had increased in BAT after cold exposure.
source: Using real-time PCR, we found that both Mpc1 and Mpc2 expression had increased in BAT (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by gene expression data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Ucp1 and Dio2 expression increased in BAT after cold exposure.
source: This was accompanied by induction of thermogenic transcripts, including Ucp1 and Dio2, while Cidea expression was unchanged (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by gene expression data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Cidea expression was unchanged in BAT after cold exposure.
source: This was accompanied by induction of thermogenic transcripts, including Ucp1 and Dio2, while Cidea expression was unchanged (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by gene expression data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Thermoneutrality (30°C) decreased Mpc2 and Ucp1 expression in BAT.
source: In contrast, thermoneutrality (30°C) decreased Mpc2 and Ucp1 expression, while Mpc1 was unchanged (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by gene expression data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Thermoneutrality (30°C) left Mpc1 expression unchanged in BAT.
source: In contrast, thermoneutrality (30°C) decreased Mpc2 and Ucp1 expression, while Mpc1 was unchanged (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by gene expression data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Increased protein expression of MPC1, MPC2, and UCP1 was observed in BAT after 1 week of cold exposure.
source: Similarly, we saw increased protein expression of MPC1, MPC2, and UCP1 in BAT after 1 week of cold exposure (Figure 3C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 3C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Cytochrome C remained unchanged after cold exposure in BAT.
source: In contrast, another mitochondrial protein, Cytochrome C, remained unchanged after a similar cold exposure.
evidence: This is supported by western blot data.

claim: The increased expression of MPC1 may provide additional pyruvate transport and oxidative capacity for sustaining prolonged thermogenesis in BAT.
source: The increased expression of MPC1 may provide additional pyruvate transport and oxidative capacity for sustaining prolonged thermogenesis in BAT.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the observed increase in MPC1 expression.

claim: Loss of MPC1 resulted in destabilization of MPC2 in BAT.
source: To test whether loss of MPC1 resulted in destabilization of MPC2, we completed western blot analysis and found that MPC2 was also depleted in BAT of Mpc1F/F::Ucp1Cre mice (Figure 3E and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 3E and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Loss of MPC1 and MPC2 was specific to brown adipose tissue in Mpc1F/F::Ucp1Cre mice.
source: To address whether loss of MPC1 and MPC2 was specific to brown adipose tissue, we also completed western blot analysis on iWAT, and found similar levels of both MPC1 and MPC2 (Figure 3F and Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 3F and Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Mpc1F/F::Ucp1Cre mice had significantly lower core body temperatures when compared to their Mpc1F/F littermate controls upon 5 hours of cold exposure.
source: Upon 5 hours of cold exposure, Mpc1F/F::Ucp1Cre mice had significantly lower core body temperatures when compared to their Mpc1F/F littermate controls, suggesting that mitochondrial pyruvate transport is essential for optimal thermogenesis (Figure 3G).
evidence: This is supported by body temperature measurements shown in Figure 3G.

claim: The cold sensitivity in Mpc1F/F::Ucp1Cre mice was not due to depletion of glucose.
source: The cold sensitivity was not due to depletion of glucose, as blood glucose levels were similar between Mpc1F/F and Mpc1F/F::Ucp1Cre mice (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is supported by blood glucose measurements shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Mpc1F/F::Ucp1Cre mice had glucose excursion curves that were impaired when compared to their Mpc1F/F littermate controls.
source: To determine whether loss of MPC1 led to changes in systemic glucose metabolism, we completed a glucose tolerance test at room temperature (23°C) or with cold (4°C), and found that Mpc1F/F::Ucp1Cre mice had glucose excursion curves that were impaired when compared to their Mpc1F/F littermate controls (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by glucose tolerance test data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The loss of MPC1 in BAT did not change body composition of chow-fed mice.
source: The loss of MPC1 in BAT did not change body composition of chow-fed mice (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by body composition data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: CL-316,243 administration resulted in a greater decrease in blood glucose levels in Mpc1F/F controls when compared to Mpc1F/F::Ucp1Cre mice.
source: We also found that CL-316,243 administration resulted in a greater decrease in blood glucose levels in Mpc1F/F controls when compared to Mpc1F/F::Ucp1Cre mice (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by blood glucose measurements shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Insulin sensitivity was similar between Mpc1F/F and Mpc1F/F::Ucp1Cre mice.
source: In contrast, insulin sensitivity was similar between the two groups as demonstrated by % change in glucose over time (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by insulin tolerance test data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Histological analysis by H and E staining of BAT, iWAT, eWAT, and liver showed little to no differences in tissue morphology between the control and MPC1 null mice.
source: Histological analysis by H and E staining of BAT, iWAT, eWAT, and liver showed little to no differences in tissue morphology between the control and MPC1 null mice (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is supported by histological data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Mpc1F/F::Ucp1Cre mice had reduced expression of Ucp1, Dio2, Elovl3, and Pparg2 relative to Mpc1F/F control mice.
source: Given that Mpc1F/F::Ucp1Cre mice had a cold sensitive phenotype, we measured gene expression of thermogenic-associated transcripts in BAT, and found that Mpc1F/F::Ucp1Cre mice had reduced expression of Ucp1, Dio2, Elovl3, and Pparg2 relative to Mpc1F/F control mice (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is supported by gene expression data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: No changes were observed in expression of genes involved in de novo lipogenesis and ketolysis in BAT of Mpc1F/F::Ucp1Cre mice.
source: No changes were observed in expression of genes involved in de novo lipogenesis and ketolysis (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by gene expression data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Mpc1F/F::Ucp1Cre mice had increased levels of the fatty acid transporter CD36.
source: While we observed increased levels of the fatty acid transporter CD36 in Mpc1F/F::Ucp1Cre mice, we saw no differences in Pnpla2 (Atgl), Cpt1b, Cpt2, or Agpat2 expression (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is supported by gene expression data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: No differences in Pnpla2 (Atgl), Cpt1b, Cpt2, or Agpat2 expression were observed in BAT of Mpc1F/F::Ucp1Cre mice.
source: While we observed increased levels of the fatty acid transporter CD36 in Mpc1F/F::Ucp1Cre mice, we saw no differences in Pnpla2 (Atgl), Cpt1b, Cpt2, or Agpat2 expression (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is supported by gene expression data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: By gene expression, there is no compensatory upregulation of fatty acid oxidation in brown adipose tissue of mice lacking MPC1.
source: This suggested that by gene expression, we do not see a compensatory upregulation of fatty acid oxidation in brown adipose tissue of mice lacking MPC1.
evidence: This is an inference based on the gene expression data.

claim: No compensatory changes in thermogenic gene expression were found in iWAT of Mpc1F/F::Ucp1Cre mice.
source: We also did not find compensatory changes in thermogenic gene expression in iWAT (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is supported by gene expression data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1D.

claim: RER was significantly elevated in Mpc1F/F::Ucp1Cre mice when compared to controls at 6°C.
source: Although we did not find a significant reduction in energy expenditure or change in activity with the loss of MPC1, RER was significantly elevated in Mpc1F/F::Ucp1Cre mice when compared to controls (Figure 4E, F and G).
evidence: This is supported by CLAMS data shown in Figure 4E, F and G.

claim: No significant reduction in energy expenditure was found with the loss of MPC1 at 6°C.
source: Although we did not find a significant reduction in energy expenditure or change in activity with the loss of MPC1, RER was significantly elevated in Mpc1F/F::Ucp1Cre mice when compared to controls (Figure 4E, F and G).
evidence: This is supported by CLAMS data shown in Figure 4E, F and G.

claim: No change in activity was found with the loss of MPC1 at 6°C.
source: Although we did not find a significant reduction in energy expenditure or change in activity with the loss of MPC1, RER was significantly elevated in Mpc1F/F::Ucp1Cre mice when compared to controls (Figure 4E, F and G).
evidence: This is supported by CLAMS data shown in Figure 4E, F and G.

claim: Both Mpc1F/F and Mpc1F/F::Ucp1Cre mice had reduction in RER at 6°C, suggesting a metabolic switch toward fat utilization.
source: Notably, both Mpc1F/F and Mpc1F/F::Ucp1Cre mice had reduction in RER, suggesting a metabolic switch toward fat utilization.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed reduction in RER.

claim: Loss of MPC1 led to destabilization and loss of MPC2 in brown adipocytes.
source: This allowed us to generate Mpc1 null cells on day 1 of differentiation as confirmed by western blot (Figure 5A) and gene expression analysis (Figure 5B). Although Mpc2 mRNA was not changed (Figure 5B), loss of MPC1 led to destabilization and loss of MPC2 (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is supported by western blot and gene expression data shown in Figure 5A and 5B.

claim: Mpc2 mRNA was not changed with loss of MPC1 in brown adipocytes.
source: Although Mpc2 mRNA was not changed (Figure 5B), loss of MPC1 led to destabilization and loss of MPC2 (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is supported by gene expression data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: After 5 hours of CL-316,243 stimulation, there was extensive M+3 labeling of pyruvate, lactate, serine, alanine, and M+6 labeling of glucose-6-phosphate and M+5 labeling of ribose-5-phosphate in both control and Mpc1 null cells.
source: After 5 hours of CL-316,243 stimulation, we found extensive M+3 labeling of pyruvate, lactate, serine, alanine, and M+6 labeling of glucose-6-phosphate and M+5 labeling of ribose-5-phosphate in both control and Mpc1 null cells (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is supported by isotopic tracing data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Greater incorporation of glucose-derived carbons into serine was found in Mpc1 null cells treated with CL-316,243.
source: Notably, we found greater incorporation of glucose-derived carbons into serine in Mpc1 null cells treated with CL-316,243.
evidence: This is supported by isotopic tracing data.

claim: CL-316,243 treatment led to a dramatic increase in lactate, pyruvate, and ribose-5-phosphate in both control and Mpc1 null cells.
source: CL-316,243 treatment led to a dramatic increase in lactate, pyruvate, and ribose-5-phosphate in both control and Mpc1 null cells.
evidence: This is supported by metabolite abundance measurements.

claim: CL-316,243 treated MPC1 null brown adipocytes had a greater increase in steady state pyruvate levels.
source: In contrast, CL-316,243 treated MPC1 null brown adipocytes had a greater increase in steady state pyruvate levels (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is supported by metabolite abundance measurements shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Upon stimulation with CL-316,243, greater levels of M+3 pyruvate and M+3 lactate were found in the media, with no distinguishable differences between control and knockout cells.
source: Upon stimulation with CL-316,243, we found greater levels of M+3 pyruvate and M+3 lactate in the media, with no distinguishable differences between control and knockout cells (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by media metabolite measurements shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Basal levels of M+3 pyruvate and M+3 lactate were elevated in MPC1 null cells.
source: However, basal levels of M+3 pyruvate and M+3 lactate were elevated in MPC1 null cells.
evidence: This is supported by media metabolite measurements.

claim: CL-316,243 treatment increased flux through pyruvate dehydrogenase (PDH), which was illustrated by increased M+2 isotopologues of citrate/isocitrate, α-ketoglutarate, succinate, fumarate, and malate.
source: CL-316,243 treatment increased flux through pyruvate dehydrogenase (PDH), which was illustrated by increased M+2 isotopologues of citrate/isocitrate, α-ketoglutarate, succinate, fumarate, and malate (Figure 6A and B and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by isotopic tracing data shown in Figure 6A, B and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A.

claim: M+3 aspartate increased with CL-316,243 treatment in control cells.
source: We found that M+3 aspartate, increased with CL-316,243 treatment in control cells, while MPC1 null cells had reduced M+3 aspartate.
evidence: This is supported by isotopic tracing data.

claim: MPC1 null cells had reduced M+3 aspartate.
source: We found that M+3 aspartate, increased with CL-316,243 treatment in control cells, while MPC1 null cells had reduced M+3 aspartate.
evidence: This is supported by isotopic tracing data.

claim: Loss of MPC1 severely attenuates incorporation of glucose-derived carbons into the TCA cycle, leading to reduced steady state levels of both fumarate and malate.
source: Together we found that loss of MPC1 severely attenuates incorporation of glucose-derived carbons into the TCA cycle, leading to reduced steady state levels of both fumarate and malate (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is supported by isotopic tracing and metabolite abundance data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: CL-316,243 treatment increased M+2 malate and M+2 glutamate in Mpc1F/F control cells when incubated with 13C-U-palmitate.
source: We found that CL-316,243 treatment increased M+2 malate and M+2 glutamate in Mpc1F/F control cells.
evidence: This is supported by isotopic tracing data with 13C-U-palmitate.

claim: The loss of MPC1 resulted in greater levels of both M+2 malate and M+2 glutamate in the basal and CL-316,243 treated group when incubated with 13C-U-palmitate.
source: However, the loss of MPC1 resulted in greater levels of both M+2 malate and M+2 glutamate in the basal and CL-316,243 treated group.
evidence: This is supported by isotopic tracing data with 13C-U-palmitate.

claim: Loss of MPC1 promotes a compensatory increase in mitochondrial fatty acid oxidation.
source: These studies would suggest that loss of MPC1 promotes a compensatory increase in mitochondrial fatty acid oxidation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed increase in fatty acid-derived TCA cycle intermediates.

claim: Acute inhibition of MPC with UK-5099 increased oxygen consumption in brown adipocytes in the basal state and in response to CL-316,243 treatment.
source: To test whether acute inhibition of MPC alters respiratory capacity in brown adipocytes, we treated cells with MPC inhibitor UK-5099, and surprisingly found increased oxygen consumption in the basal state and in response to CL-316,243 treatment (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is supported by oxygen consumption measurements shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Inclusion of etomoxir with UK-5099 treatment led to a dramatic drop in oxygen consumption in brown adipocytes.
source: To test whether fatty acid oxidation was required for the rise in basal oxygen consumption, we included etomoxir with UK-5099 treatment, which led to a dramatic drop in oxygen consumption.
evidence: This is supported by oxygen consumption measurements.

claim: Brown fat mitochondria from Mpc1F/F::UCP1Cre mice had reduced oxygen consumption when challenged with pyruvate/malate.
source: Mitochondria were incubated with defined respiratory substrates, including pyruvate/malate or palmitoyl-carnitine, and found that oxygen consumption increased in Mpc1F/F brown adipocytes. In contrast, brown fat mitochondria from Mpc1F/F::UCP1Cre mice had reduced oxygen consumption when challenged with pyruvate/malate (Figure 7C).
evidence: This is supported by mitochondrial oxygen consumption measurements shown in Figure 7C.

claim: Upon incubation with palmitoyl-carnitine, MPC1 null mitochondria showed a compensatory increase in oxygen consumption rate.
source: However, upon incubation with palmitoyl-carnitine, MPC1 null cells showed a compensatory increase in oxygen consumption rate when provided palmitoyl-carnitine.
evidence: This is supported by mitochondrial oxygen consumption measurements.

claim: When ADP or Succinate was added, MPC1 null mitochondria had reduced respiratory capacity relative to Mpc1F/F controls.
source: When ADP or Succinate was added, MPC1 null mitochondria had reduced respiratory capacity relative to Mpc1F/F controls (Figure 7D).
evidence: This is supported by mitochondrial oxygen consumption measurements shown in Figure 7D.

claim: Similar increase in respiration was found in Mpc1F/F and Mpc1F/F::Ucp1Cre brown adipocytes when mitochondria were incubated with ascorbate and TMPD.
source: To test whether complex IV-dependent respiration was altered, we incubated mitochondria with ascorbate and TMPD, and found similar increase in respiration in Mpc1F/F and Mpc1F/F::Ucp1Cre brown adipocytes.
evidence: This is supported by mitochondrial oxygen consumption measurements.

claim: Metabolite analysis of serum showed an increase in 3-hydroxybutyrate and adenosine in cold challenged Mpc1F/F::Ucp1Cre mice.
source: Metabolite analysis of serum showed an increase in 3-hydroxybutyrate and adenosine (Figure 8A), while metabolite analysis of BAT showed that cold exposed Mpc1F/F::Ucp1Cre mice had elevated 3-hydroxybutyrate, 2-hydroxybutyrate, adenosine 5'-monophosphate (AMP), 2-monopalmitoylglycerol, malonic acid, and cis-acotinic acid relative to Mpc1F/F mice (Figure 8B).
evidence: This is supported by metabolomics data shown in Figure 8A.

claim: Cold exposed Mpc1F/F::Ucp1Cre mice had elevated 3-hydroxybutyrate, 2-hydroxybutyrate, adenosine 5'-monophosphate (AMP), 2-monopalmitoylglycerol, malonic acid, and cis-acotinic acid in BAT relative to Mpc1F/F mice.
source: Metabolite analysis of serum showed an increase in 3-hydroxybutyrate and adenosine (Figure 8A), while metabolite analysis of BAT showed that cold exposed Mpc1F/F::Ucp1Cre mice had elevated 3-hydroxybutyrate, 2-hydroxybutyrate, adenosine 5'-monophosphate (AMP), 2-monopalmitoylglycerol, malonic acid, and cis-acotinic acid relative to Mpc1F/F mice (Figure 8B).
evidence: This is supported by metabolomics data shown in Figure 8B.

claim: Analysis of the top 25 BAT metabolites showed a significant increase in 3-hydroxybutyrate in Mpc1F/F::Ucp1Cre mice.
source: Analysis of the top 25 BAT metabolites showed a significant increase in 3-hydroxybutyrate, while TCA cycle intermediates such as succinic, citric, and isocitric acid were decreased (Figure 8B).
evidence: This is supported by metabolomics data shown in Figure 8B.

claim: TCA cycle intermediates such as succinic, citric, and isocitric acid were decreased in BAT of Mpc1F/F::Ucp1Cre mice.
source: Analysis of the top 25 BAT metabolites showed a significant increase in 3-hydroxybutyrate, while TCA cycle intermediates such as succinic, citric, and isocitric acid were decreased (Figure 8B).
evidence: This is supported by metabolomics data shown in Figure 8B.

claim: Cold exposure elevated serum 3-hydroxybutyrate levels in Mpc1F/F control mice.
source: To test whether ketones were induced with cold exposure, we measured serum 3-hydroxybutyrate in Mpc1F/F and Mpc1F/F::Ucp1Cre mice, and found that cold exposure elevated serum 3-hydroxybutyrate levels in Mpc1F/F control mice (Figure 8C).
evidence: This is supported by serum 3-hydroxybutyrate measurements shown in Figure 8C.

claim: Loss of MPC1 in brown adipose tissue led to blood 3-hydroxybutyrate levels that surpassed those of control mice in the cold.
source: Notably, loss of MPC1 in brown adipose tissue led to blood 3-hydroxybutyrate levels that surpassed those of control mice in the cold (Figure 8C).
evidence: This is supported by serum 3-hydroxybutyrate measurements shown in Figure 8C.

claim: Fasn, Acaca (ACC1), and Acly, genes involved in fatty acid synthesis, were downregulated in livers of Mpc1F/F::Ucp1Cre mice.
source: While Fasn, Acaca (ACC1), and Acly, genes involved in fatty acid synthesis, were downregulated in Mpc1F/F::Ucp1Cre mice, Cpt1b, Cpt2, and Acadm (fatty acid oxidation genes) were increased, followed by increased levels of Hmgcs2 which is directly involved in ketogenesis (Figure 8D).
evidence: This is supported by gene expression data shown in Figure 8D.

claim: Cpt1b, Cpt2, and Acadm (fatty acid oxidation genes) were increased in livers of Mpc1F/F::Ucp1Cre mice.
source: While Fasn, Acaca (ACC1), and Acly, genes involved in fatty acid synthesis, were downregulated in Mpc1F/F::Ucp1Cre mice, Cpt1b, Cpt2, and Acadm (fatty acid oxidation genes) were increased, followed by increased levels of Hmgcs2 which is directly involved in ketogenesis (Figure 8D).
evidence: This is supported by gene expression data shown in Figure 8D.

claim: Hmgcs2, which is directly involved in ketogenesis, was increased in livers of Mpc1F/F::Ucp1Cre mice.
source: While Fasn, Acaca (ACC1), and Acly, genes involved in fatty acid synthesis, were downregulated in Mpc1F/F::Ucp1Cre mice, Cpt1b, Cpt2, and Acadm (fatty acid oxidation genes) were increased, followed by increased levels of Hmgcs2 which is directly involved in ketogenesis (Figure 8D).
evidence: This is supported by gene expression data shown in Figure 8D.

claim: Upstream regulators of ketogenesis, including Ppar and Pppargc1a, were not changed in the livers of Mpc1F/F::Ucp1Cre mice.
source: In contrast, upstream regulators of ketogenesis, including Ppar and Pppargc1a, were not changed in the livers (Figure 8—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by gene expression data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1A.

claim: No notable differences were seen in serum free fatty acids between Mpc1F/F and Mpc1F/F::Ucp1Cre mice.
source: No notable differences were seen in serum free fatty acids (Figure 8—figure supplement 1B), suggesting that activation of ketogenesis is likely contributing to rise in 3-hydroxybutyrate levels.
evidence: This is supported by serum free fatty acid measurements shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Activation of ketogenesis is likely contributing to rise in 3-hydroxybutyrate levels in Mpc1F/F::Ucp1Cre mice.
source: No notable differences were seen in serum free fatty acids (Figure 8—figure supplement 1B), suggesting that activation of ketogenesis is likely contributing to rise in 3-hydroxybutyrate levels.
evidence: This is an inference based on the lack of change in serum free fatty acids and increased ketogenic gene expression.

claim: No changes in expression of ketogenic pathway were found in iWAT of Mpc1F/F::Ucp1Cre mice.
source: In addition, we did not find changes in expression of ketogenic pathway in iWAT (Figure 8—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by gene expression data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Activation of hepatic ketone production provides an additional compensatory mechanism to counteract the inability to directly oxidize pyruvate in the BAT mitochondria.
source: Together, these findings suggest that activation of hepatic ketone production provides an additional compensatory mechanism to counteract the inability to directly oxidize pyruvate in the BAT mitochondria.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed increase in ketogenic gene expression and 3-hydroxybutyrate levels.

claim: There is a prevailing view that BAT relies primarily on free fatty acids as the primary source of energy for brown fat thermogenesis.
source: There is a prevailing view that BAT relies primarily on free fatty acids as the primary source of energy for brown fat thermogenesis.
evidence: This is a statement about the prevailing view in the field.

claim: Cold activation of BAT leads to utilization of other substrates besides fatty acids, such as glucose, amino acids and acylcarnitines.
source: However, it has been demonstrated in the past that cold activation of BAT leads to utilization of other substrates besides fatty acids, such as glucose, amino acids (López-Soriano et al., 1988; Yoneshiro et al., 2019) and acylcarnitines (Simcox et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The inability to transport pyruvate leads to compensatory metabolic programming towards fatty acid oxidation.
source: These effects highlight that the inability to transport pyruvate, leads to compensatory metabolic programming towards fatty acid oxidation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed increase in fatty acid oxidation in MPC1 null cells.

claim: There may be compensation through glutamine oxidation, transamination of alanine to pyruvate in the mitochondria, glutamine anaplerosis via glutamate to α-ketoglutarate by glutaminase and glutamate dehydrogenase enzymes, or conversion of glutamine-derived malate to pyruvate by mitochondrial malic enzyme.
source: In addition, there may be compensation through glutamine oxidation, transamination of alanine to pyruvate in the mitochondria, glutamine anaplerosis via glutamate to α-ketoglutarate by glutaminase and glutamate dehydrogenase enzymes, or conversion of glutamine-derived malate to pyruvate by mitochondrial malic enzyme (Bender and Martinou, 2016; Gray et al., 2015; McCommis et al., 2015; Schell et al., 2014; Vacanti et al., 2014; Yang et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a speculation about potential compensatory mechanisms supported by citations.

claim: Ketogenesis occurs primarily in the liver during exercise or prolonged fasting, and more recently was found to be a cold-induced metabolite.
source: Ketogenesis occurs primarily in the liver during exercise or prolonged fasting, and more recently was found to be a cold-induced metabolite (Newman and Verdin, 2014b; Newman and Verdin, 2014a; Wang et al., 2019).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Ketones can be exported to extrahepatic tissues for further oxidation as they are rich energy sources.
source: Ketones can be exported to extrahepatic tissues for further oxidation as they are rich energy sources.
evidence: This is established knowledge about ketone metabolism.

claim: In order for ketones to be catabolized in peripheral tissues they have to utilize OXCT1 for import and succinyl-CoA to donate coenzyme-A.
source: However, in order for ketones to be catabolized in peripheral tissues they have to utilize OXCT1 for import and succinyl-CoA to donate coenzyme-A.
evidence: This is established knowledge about ketone catabolism.

claim: Mpc1F/F::Ucp1Cre mice had lower levels of TCA cycle intermediates compared to their littermate controls, including succinic acid, citric acid, and malic acid.
source: In the BAT metabolomics analysis, Mpc1F/F::Ucp1Cre mice had lower levels of TCA cycle intermediates compared to their littermate controls, including succinic acid, citric acid, and malic acid.
evidence: This is supported by metabolomics data.

claim: Lower levels of TCA cycle intermediates in Mpc1F/F::Ucp1Cre mice suggest that oxidative metabolism is limited in the absence of MPC1.
source: This would suggest that oxidative metabolism is limited in the absence of MPC1.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed lower levels of TCA cycle intermediates.

claim: BAT utilizes ketones for thermogenesis.
source: One likely explanation is that BAT utilizes ketones for thermogenesis.
evidence: This is a speculation about the role of ketones in BAT.

claim: Ketones can promote energy expenditure, mitochondrial biogenesis, and stimulate the expression of Ucp1 in WAT.
source: Alternatively, ketones can promote energy expenditure, mitochondrial biogenesis, and stimulate the expression of Ucp1 in WAT (Srivastava et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.
